focus: Frontier node F-2-005 (depth 2, scope .skilled/skills/system-skilled-bots/runtime/): What is the smallest on-disk memory store for a few people on one machine: one JSONL per person plus a per-bot overlay?
noveltyJustification: 14 of 16 findings are new external evidence from the state layout and three reference stores; 2 are new design inferences that reuse the existing shared/per-identity split.
keyQuestions: How do the reference repos build bot memory (per-bot and shared) and skills (written, recorded from a demonstration, proposed from use), and how would those map onto Skilled skills and the spec-kit?
answeredQuestions: What is the smallest on-disk memory store for a few people on one machine: one JSONL per person plus a per-bot overlay?
ruledOut: A second SQLite database for memory
Keying memory by repository identity only

label: The runtime resolves a user-level state root: pinned SKILLED_BOTS_STATE_ROOT outranks the checkout's bots/config.json stateRoot, which outranks ${XDG_STATE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/state}/system-skilled-bots.

The layout is already two-level: per-identity folders (requests, leases, switches, needs-you, records, installs, receipts) under {stateRoot}/{identityKey}/, and shared entries (index, registered-roots, authority) directly under the root.
Every state folder is created owner-only with mode 0o700, the same rule the env-secret guard applies to its own state.
One JSON file per thing is the existing convention: recordFile is {records}/{runId}.json and needsYouFile is {needsYou}/{itemId}.json, both guarded by isSafeSegment.
The status index is the one exception: a SQLite database with tables meta, generations, runs, deliveries, items and retired, because it answers cross-identity queries a folder of files cannot.
The runtime has no memory store at all: grep for memory across runtime/lib/*.ts returns zero hits.
The runtime has no per-person identity: operator is only a role word (approval origin, failure class, kill switch) and every state path is keyed by repository identity owner/name.

OpenBot scopes memory by organization and person: the collection path is /api/v2/organizations/{organizationId}/people/{personId}/memories, and a memory named from another organization is answered as not found.
OpenBot keeps no memory at all for a single-person deployment: a single-person OpenBot keeps no memory and every operation answers not found.
OpenBot's per-bot dimension is the source, not the store: MemorySource.botId is the Bot that reads it and the only one that recalls what it read in.
OpenGhost keeps one bounded memory for the user across all chats: LIMITS text 400, records 60, crowded 28, chars 3600, and a model rewrites it shorter as one whole once crowded.
openhuman has no user root before sign-in: user_root returns None when the config path is not under users/ or the id is the pre-login id.

The smallest store that fits the existing layout is one JSON file per person at the shared level plus one per-bot overlay inside the identity folder: {stateRoot}/memory/{personId}.json and {stateRoot}/{identityKey}/memory/{botId}.json.

JSONL is the wrong format here: writeStateAtomic already does a whole-file temp write, fsync and rename, and writeStateIfChangedAtomic skips an unchanged write, so a JSON array per person gets atomicity for free.

The per-bot overlay makes recall cheap: recall reads the person file plus the bot's overlay and dedupes by fact id, the same two-file read delivery.ts already performs for a run record plus its needs-you item.

A single-person install should keep no memory file at all, matching OpenBot: the person file is created on the first fact a bot forms, so an install with one person and no review never grows a memory folder.

reason: The runtime's atomic write helper is whole-file, so JSONL buys nothing and costs a new append path plus a line-level parser.

direction: One JSON file per fact, matching records/ and needs-you/
reason: A few hundred facts would become a few hundred files and recall would read the whole folder on every run.

direction: A second SQLite database for memory
reason: The index is SQLite for cross-identity queries; memory is read whole by one bot at a time, so a database adds a schema and migration for no query benefit.

direction: Key memory by repository identity only
reason: That is today's key, and it makes a person's facts vanish when they move to another checkout.
